<reason>Both sides were skilled and disciplined on evidence, but B did more damage to the motion's core mechanism. A's strongest early hits (1099s are annual tax forms, not contemporaneous UI wage reports; partial-unemployment precedent) were real, but B's central objection — that earnings records cannot establish involuntary loss for self-scheduling workers — was never neutralized. Under pressure, A's coverage kept shrinking from "millions accrue credits" to "the deactivated and market exits," and B converted that concession into a clean ledger: regressive costs on many low earners, benefits for a narrow few, adjudicated on data written by the premium-payer. B's "who writes the log?" incentive point went unanswered, the safe-harbor pledge was refused, and B's closing turned A's own van-driver image (injured claimants are unavailable for work, so UI wouldn't pay them) plus the fire-pool distinction into a crisp decision rule. A's execution was cleaner — B had two clipped turns and dodged A's pointed "how many more years must workers wait" question — which keeps the margin modest, but B won the central technical clash and crystallized it better.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1/2 sequence: "who writes the log?" exposed that experience-rating incentivizes platforms to quietly starve workers rather than deactivate them, and B4 then rebuilt the whole comparison from A's own answers — the narrowed claimant set, trip-by-trip adjudication of voluntary scheduling, and gross-vs-net earnings undercutting "working always pays more" — forcing A's "simple reporting standard" to become a claims bureaucracy A never acknowledged.</best_rebuttal>
